regions.evidence: Asphalt strip between a dark longitudinal band (left polygon edge) and the thick solid white lane line on its right (right polygon edge). The stop bar runs continuously across it from the median-island kerb to the right kerb, so this is part of the stop-controlled carriageway. No bicycle symbol, green paint, parking stalls or parked cars are visible in the sunlit part near the stop bar. No arrow is visible in this strip, though r2 carries one at the same station. The dark band at the left edge is not a lane line: it runs straight on through the crosswalk beyond the stop bar, so it is likely a pavement seam or joint. Pavement continues about 1.3-1.5 m further left to the actual median-island kerb, so the lane is likely about 4 m kerb-to-line, wider than the 2.54 m polygon. The downstream ~60% of the polygon lies in deep building shadow; only the lane line on its right stays traceable there.

The stop bar crosses the lane. The lower part of the polygon is in building shadow, where only the two bounding lines are faintly visible.

regions.evidence: Narrow strip, about 1.4 m, between the thin solid white line and the right kerb. It contains a localized green-painted patch about 9-11 m upstream of the stop bar (green appears nowhere else along the shadow edge, so it is likely paint rather than a colour fringe). Short white dashes beyond the stop bar and crosswalk continue in line with this strip through the intersection, consistent with a dashed bike-lane extension. No bicycle symbol is readable: a tree shadow covers much of the strip near the stop bar, and building shadow covers the downstream part. Downstream the kerb position cannot be traced in the shadow. A car sits about 7 m right of the thin line further back, so the kerb/lay-by layout may widen there; this strip is only supported near the stop bar.

regions.evidence: r1's left edge follows a continuous bright longitudinal line, read as the centre line. On the other side of it are the opposing approach's lanes, whose turn arrows point toward the junction. The left ~3.5 m of r1 is uniform asphalt with no parked objects: a SB travel lane leaving the junction. About 64% of the way across, a faint longitudinal line separates it from the right ~2 m. That right part holds a row of three cars parked end to end along the kerb, so it is a parking lane, not travel pavement. Beyond the kerb are tree-shadowed sidewalk/plaza, brick paving and buildings. The reverse look-back street view shows the same arrangement on this side of the double yellow line: one travel lane, then a solid white edge line, then cars parked at the kerb, then the sidewalk with café seating. r1 is therefore supported as a travel facility, but it covers one motor-vehicle lane plus a parking strip; only about 3.5 m of its 5.5 m width is travel lane. Most of it lies in building shadow.
